w: Whitby Abbey began as a 7th-century monastery, later a Benedictine house, its church on the East Cliff above the North Sea. Henry VIII's men seized its lands in the 1530s-40s Dissolution, but sailors still use the ruin as a landmark. Grade I listed, with a site museum in Cholmley House, run by English Heritage.
s: 7th-century monastery ruins above Whitby's East Cliff
_facts: Grade I listed ruin, cared for by English Heritage
Site museum housed in 17th-century Cholmley House

w: St Mary's was founded around 1110, though most of its interior dates from the late 18th century, and it stands Grade I listed on Whitby's east cliff by the ruined abbey. The 199 Church Steps climb up to it from the town, and its graveyard, overlooking the mouth of the River Esk, set a scene in Bram Stoker's Dracula.
s: 199 steps up to the church in Bram Stoker's Dracula
_facts: Graveyard used as a setting in Stoker's Dracula

w: The Captain Cook Memorial Museum occupies Walker's House, home of shipowner Captain John Walker, to whom a young James Cook was apprenticed in 1746. Cook lodged here as an apprentice, then returned to visit in the winter of 1771-72, fresh from his first great voyage of exploration.
s: Walker's House, where the young Cook once lodged
_facts: Cook apprenticed to Captain John Walker in 1746
Cook lodged there, revisited winter 1771-72 after his first voyage

w: Whitby Lighthouse stands on Ling Hill, on the coast southeast of the town beyond Saltwick Bay, and is run by Trinity House. To keep it distinct from Whitby's two harbour lighthouses, sailors reading Admiralty charts often call it Whitby High - the outer marker for ships working this stretch of Yorkshire coast.
s: Whitby High: the outer light beyond Saltwick Bay
_facts: Located on Ling Hill, beyond Saltwick Bay
Also known as Whitby High to distinguish it from the two harbour lights

w: Old St Stephen's is a redundant Anglican church set on a hillside in Fylingdales, looking down over Robin Hood's Bay near Whitby. No longer used for regular worship, it is Grade I listed and kept by the Churches Conservation Trust, a quiet survivor among the parish churches that once served this stretch of coast.
s: Redundant Grade I church above Robin Hood's Bay
_facts: Cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust

w: Whitby East Pier Lighthouse has guarded one side of the harbour entrance since 1855, the newer and shorter of Whitby's two pier lights at 54 feet. Around 1914 the East Pier was extended some 500 feet further out to sea with a new beacon at its tip, and both towers had their lights modernised again in 2011.
s: 1855 lighthouse marking one of Whitby's two harbour piers
_facts: 54 feet tall, shorter of Whitby's two pier lighthouses
East Pier extended c.1914 with a new beacon
